stories.headline: Trump claims 250% tariff threat stopped India-Pakistan war
stories.title: Trump claims 250% tariff threat stopped India-Pakistan war
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Donald Trump says he threatened India and Pakistan with 250% tariffs to stop fighting, but India maintains the ceasefire followed a Pakistani military request.

US President Donald Trump has once again claimed that his threat to impose 250 per cent tariffs on India and Pakistan helped bring their military confrontation to an end, renewing a claim that New Delhi has repeatedly disputed.
Speaking at a campaign rally, Trump said he warned both nuclear-armed neighbours that they would lose access to trade with the United States if they continued fighting.
“You stop India and Pakistan, two nuclear nations,” Trump said, describing what he portrayed as a direct intervention to prevent further escalation.
He claimed that he threatened both countries with tariffs of 250 per cent, adding that the warning angered their leadership but eventually stopped the fighting.
“They got very upset, very angry; they stopped shooting, and the war was over,” Trump said.
He also repeated his claim that 11 aircraft had been shot down during the confrontation.
Trump went on to cite his claimed diplomatic interventions as evidence of his role in resolving international conflicts, expressing frustration that he had not received the Nobel Peace Prize.

India has consistently rejected Trump's account of the ceasefire, maintaining that the understanding to stop military action was reached through direct military communication between the two countries.
According to India's stated position, Pakistan's Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) contacted his Indian counterpart to request a halt to hostilities.
New Delhi has also disputed Trump's claim about 11 aircraft being shot down.
The disagreement over the ceasefire's origins has persisted despite Trump's repeated assertions that his trade threats helped end the confrontation.

stories.headline: Beyond the LAC: India’s Strategic Contest With China in the Himalayas
stories.title: Beyond the LAC: India’s Strategic Contest With China in the Himalayas
stories.summary: From Doklam to Galwan: The Changing Rules of Border Competition Post-Doklam and Galwan clashes, it was very clear that the Line of Actual Control was no longer merely a disputed… The post Beyond the LAC: India’s Strategic Contest With China in the Himalayas appeared first on India Narrative .
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Post-Doklam and Galwan clashes, it was very clear that the Line of Actual Control was no longer merely a disputed frontier marked by competing maps and patrols, but now it’s a permanent contest of infrastructure, surveillance, military readiness, diplomacy, and national resilience.

From Doklam to Galwan, India has learned that the central challenge from China is not always a dramatic assault across the Himalayas, but it’s the gradual alteration of facts on the ground, which is often below the threshold of open war.
The latest phase of India-China engagement offers cautious reasons for optimism.

We know that at the 25th round of Special Representatives talks held in Beijing on 25 August 2026, India and China had agreed on an eight-point consensus covering border management, military communication, boundary negotiations, trans-border rivers, trade and pilgrimage.
Yet the agreement is best understood only as a mechanism for managing rivalry and not as proof that the rivalry has ended.

The Doklam confrontation in 2017 had clearly demonstrated that a local dispute in the Bhutan-China-India trijunction could acquire wider consequences because of its proximity to the Siliguri Corridor, which is the narrow land link connecting India’s North-Eastern states with the rest of the country.
Thus, India’s decision to physically block the Chinese road construction through Bhutan reflected a clear strategic calculation and a strong stand.
Doklam had clearly exposed the changing character of Chinese border strategy.
Infrastructure was not simply a civilian development tool.

Roads, tracks, communications networks, and permanent settlements are clearly aimed at improving the PLA’s ability to reinforce contested areas rapidly and sustain itself, dominating the local tactical environment.
Then the crisis in Eastern Ladakh in 2020 made this lesson far more urgent.
The Galwan Valley clash in which soldiers from both sides were killed actually destroyed the assumption that earlier confidence-building arrangements alone could preserve peace.

stories.headline: Centre claims external conspiracy whenever it is in crisis: Dr Farooq Abdullah
stories.title: Centre claims external conspiracy whenever it is in crisis: Dr Farooq Abdullah
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 23: National Conference (NC) president Farooq Abdullah on Friday criticised the Centre over its claims of foreign involvement in protests in Delhi, accusing the Union government of invoking the narrative of an external conspiracy whenever it faces a political crisis. Speaking to reporters here, the former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister challenged the Centre to identify the country allegedly attempting to interfere in India’s internal affairs, questioning the basis of its claims of foreign involvement. “Whenever the government in Delhi is in danger, they see a foreign hand. They do not see their own. Who is doing it? If they say foreign (hand) is doing it, then name who is doing it. Which country is trying to do this? Tell us,” Abdullah said. He alleged that the government repeatedly attributed developments to external forces without identifying the country involved. “They don't have that name at all. Just (say) foreign hand, foreign hand! A foreign hand in everything,” the NC chief said. Abdullah’s remarks came amid questions over allegations of foreign involvement in protests in the national capital. He questioned the Centre’s approach, arguing that claims of external interference should be supported by specific details identifying the country allegedly responsible. The NC president’s comments added to the political debate over the Centre’s response to protests and its assertions about possible external involvement. Responding to a question about the escalating Middle East crisis, Abdullah called for an immediate end to the war, warning that its consequences were being felt across the world, particularly through economic hardship and inflation. He criticised US President Donald Trump over the conflict and its wider consequences, saying the continuation of hostilities was contributing to global suffering. “This is Trump's favour, bringing destruction to the world. When will he come to his senses? The whole world is suffering from hardships. Look at inflation, the poor will suffer everywhere,” Abdullah said. He urged Trump to take steps to end the conflict, arguing that the economic consequences of the war would disproportionately affect poorer sections of society. “The time has come for Trump to stop this war, and it is a matter of justice that Iran has the right to protect itself. Enough is enough; this is not a time of war now,” he added.

stories.headline: An Unusual Visit
stories.title: An Unusual Visit
stories.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India on October 20-22 was significant and unusual in several respects. First: Rubio did not visit Delhi which would have been the usual go to city for a foreign minister while visiting a country on a bilateral visit. Instead, Rubio decided to go to Mumbai and thereafter Jamnagar. Perhaps Rubio felt that as he had visited the Indian capital five months earlier in May he could go to the country’s financial capital on this occasion, especially because his focus was on economic matters. Second: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar did Rubio the courtesy of going to Mumbai to meet him. This was an extraordinary gesture on Jaishankar’s part and should have been acknowledged as such by the US side. It was therefore unprofessional on the part of US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, to have used the formulation, as reported in the Indian media, for Gor meetings with Jaishankar in Mumbai. Gor said ““We expect that Minister Dr. Jaishankar will be joining us there along with other individuals here from Delhi who will be making the trip up there to see [Mr. Rubio]”. Gor is not a professional diplomat but that is no excuse for him to have used the word “expect”. That gave an opportunity to some Opposition parties to criticise Jaishankar’s graciousness towards Gor. Third: Rubio decided to go to visit the Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) owned refinery in Jamnagar. It is not unusual for foreign dignitaries to visit Indian industrial institutions during their official or unofficial trips to India and a couple of Rubio’s predecessors have done so too. But this was the first time that a US Secretary of State did so in such a specific and pointed manner. The US side was keen to project that Rubio’s trip was designed to bolster India-US economic and commercial relations. This was underlined by Rubio’s emphasis that the Indo-US trade agreement had been almost done. As mentioned in the transcript released by the US State Department of his press meeting on October 20, Rubio’s exact words were “in what’s happening. In my perch as National Security Advisor, we care a lot about it. We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without (inaudible) agreement. I think there’s a small number of items to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly – we’re hoping; it should. And hopefully I’ve got some good news to announce fairly soon, and perhaps (inaudible) can sign it thereafter”. Around the same time President Donald Trump told the US media in an informal interaction “They want to make a deal. We’re going to make the deal. Pretty close, yeah. It’s going to be a much different kind of deal than we’ve done”. No Indian official responded to this US positivity on the deal though earlier Commerce Minister Piyuish Goyal had expressed the view that negotiations had made progress. The fact is that Rubio’s visit to India was just on the eve of the US mid-term election; it is exceedingly important for the Trump administration because the loss of even one of the chambers of the US Congress would make the remaining two years of the US President’s term very different from what it has been till now. Even though there are signs that the Republican Party is closing the gap in some important ‘races’ there is major anger among voters on inflation in the country caused, among other reasons, because of increased energy prices. That has been on account of the Iran war. The prospects of any further turmoil in the global energy market led Trump to ‘pause’ the application of the Lindsey Graham Act on Russian oil. It is in this context that Rubio’s visit to Jamnagar to urge the Ambani group to purchase Venezuelan crude for its refineries becomes relevant. It was to show that the Trump administration is going out of its way to keep the energy markets calm. At an event to mark the 250th year of US independence hosted by Gor in New York Jaishankar summarised the growth in Indo-US ties well. He said “...in the last few decades, our partnership has steadily expanded, acquiring new dimensions and new facets. The Quad, Mission 500, Pax Silica and the FORGE initiative are among some of the notable examples. And growth in the fields of energy, in defence and civil aviation sectors have actually been striking”. There is no doubt that India’s ties with the US are of great importance for India but they have received setbacks because of Trump’s actions on tariffs and immigration. Rubio sought to assuage India’s feelings on Trump’s policies and actions that have negatively impacted India since last year by clarifying that these measures did not target India but were part of US attempts to rectify its own policies which had universal applicability. These fine words cannot provide solace to those who have been at the receiving end of the weaponisation of tariffs in particular. Nor can India forget that Trump had used disparaging words against this country. All eyes will now be on the India-US trade deal. It is not clear what Trump meant when he said that it will be a “different” kind of deal than the US’s trade deals with other countries. Indian officials have not commented on this aspect at all. Does it mean that new and non-traditional concepts are being adopted for this deal?

stories.headline: Can accused get certified copies of General Security Force Court proceedings?
stories.title: Can accused get certified copies of General Security Force Court proceedings?
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 23: Upholding the constitutional validity of Rule 129 of the Border Security Force (BSF) Rules, 1969, the High Court of J&K and Ladakh has ruled that an accused tried by a Security Force Court is disentitled to certified copies of trial proceedings before confirmation of the finding and sentence, provided the statutory right to inspect the proceedings and other safeguards are available. Allowing an appeal by Ministry of Home Affairs, Inspector General Border Security Force, Director General BSF, General Security Force Court at Pantha-chowk, Srinagar and others, a division bench comprising Chief Justice DrPushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice M A Chowdhary set aside a Single Judge's decision dated April 28, 2022. In its judgment the single judge bench had declared Rule 129 unconstitutional for violating the right to a fair trial under Article 21 of the Constitution. In the decision reserved on September 24 and pronounced on October 22, the division bench held that the provision, when read harmoniously with the BSF Act and the Rules, regulates the timing of access to copies rather than denying an accused access to the trial record altogether. The case stemmed from killing of ahead Constable ChanderBhan at a BSF campus in Bandipora on November 27, 2017. A General Security Force Court (GSFC) tried Rovinder Singh, a BSF constable for the murder and for leaving his picket allegedly without orders from superior officers. The court found him guilty and awarded life imprisonment and dismissal from service, subject to statutory confirmation. During the trial, Singh sought certified copies of the challan, related documents and statements of prosecution witnesses. His request was declined under Rule 129, which provides for obtaining copies after confirmation of the finding and sentence. Singh called in question the restriction in his plea before the single bench with the contention that the denial of copies impaired his ability to prepare an effective defence. The bench accepted his plea, struck down Rule 129 and directed the GSFC to resume proceedings from the stage of conclusion of prosecution evidence, providing him with the relevant copies. Overturning the single judge’s decision, the division bench in keeping with a related supreme court’s decision underscored that the right to inspect court-martial proceedings at reasonable times could satisfy the requirements of natural justice and that an accused could not insist upon daily copies of the proceedings. The bench pointed out that Section 87 of the BSF Act makes the Indian Evidence Act applicable to Security Force Court proceedings subject to the provisions of the special legislation. It held that Rule 129 operates within this statutory framework and does not extinguish the accused's right to inspect the record. Moreover, the bench underscored that Article 21 guarantees a fair opportunity to defend oneself but does not invariably require that the opportunity take the form of possession of certified copies at every stage of a trial. Referring to Article 33 of the Constitution, the court noted that Parliament has the power to restrict or modify the application of fundamental rights to members of the armed forces and forces charged with maintaining public order to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and maintenance of discipline. The BSF Act provides for inspection of proceedings, representation and assistance during trial, review, confirmation of findings and sentences, and further statutory remedies against adverse decisions, it said. The court held Rule 129 could not be considered in isolation from these safeguards and that the distinction between proceedings awaiting confirmation and those already confirmed had a rational basis within the special statutory framework governing Security Force Courts. It said that no material had been placed before it to demonstrate that Singh had actually been prevented from inspecting the proceedings, cross-examining a material witness or raising a specific defence because of the denial of copies. Furthermore, the court noted that the “existence of a possibility that a copy may assist a defence is not sufficient to invalidate a rule which forms part of a special statutory procedure”. The court declared Rule 129 constitutionally valid and held that non-supply of certified copies before confirmation of the finding and sentence does not, by itself, violate the right to a fair trial under Article 21, while allowing the appeal assailing the single bench’s decision. The bench clarified that its judgment would have no bearing on the final adjudication of Singh's guilt or punishment and directed the competent authorities to proceed in accordance with the BSF Act and Rules. Advocate Hakim Aman Ali, Central Government counsel appeared for Border Security Force as appellants

stories.headline: Govt announces 25 crore development projects for Beerwah
stories.title: Govt announces 25 crore development projects for Beerwah
stories.summary: Budgam, Oct 23: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday said his government was making every effort to accelerate development across the Union Territory, asserting that his visit to Beerwah was aimed at reviewing and advancing key development projects in the constituency. Speaking to reporters at Beerwah tehsil, the Chief Minister said several development initiatives had been taken up in the area, with a focus on improving infrastructure, road connectivity, electricity supply and public amenities. Recalling his association with the Beerwah Assembly constituency, Omar Abdullah said he had been elected as its MLA in the 2014 Assembly elections and had remained committed to fulfilling the promises made to the people. “I have a long-standing relationship with Beerwah. When the people elected me as their representative in 2014, I promised to work for the development of the constituency. After the formation of our government, we initiated several development projects here,” he said. The Chief Minister said around ₹25 crore had been allocated for various development works in Beerwah. Of the six projects, one has been inaugurated, while foundation stones have been laid for the remaining five. He said each project was important for addressing the developmental needs of the constituency. Highlighting the completion of a long-pending public demand, Omar Abdullah said a bridge over Nallah Sukhnag, which had been damaged in the 2014 floods, had been reconstructed and handed over to the public. “The bridge was a long-pending demand of the people. I am thankful to the Deputy Chief Minister and the concerned department for completing the work within a short period. The bridge has now been handed over to the people,” he said. The Chief Minister said measures were also being taken to improve the appearance of Beerwah town. The foundation stone has been laid for a walking track and decks along the banks of Nallah Sukhnag. In addition, ₹4 crore has been earmarked for the construction and improvement of lanes and drains in the Beerwah main town. On electricity infrastructure, Omar Abdullah said the capacity of the receiving station in Beerwah would be enhanced to improve power supply to the area. He said the work was expected to be completed within five months. He added that the foundation stone had also been laid for a transformer workshop at the Beerwah receiving station, where damaged transformers could be repaired, helping improve the maintenance of the local power distribution network. Addressing concerns over road development, the Chief Minister said several road projects had been delayed due to the India-Pakistan conflict and a shortage of raw materials. He said funds had already been provided for road development and macadamisation, adding that roads approved during the current year were expected to be completed next year. Omar Abdullah also assured residents that pending development works would receive attention. Responding to the demand for a stadium in Beerwah, he said a suitable site would be identified to enable the Sports Department to take up the project. The Chief Minister also addressed concerns over the proposed diversion of traffic from the national highway passing through the centre of Beerwah town. Residents have expressed apprehensions that diverting traffic could affect local businesses and commercial activity. He said the matter had been taken up with the concerned highway authorities and that efforts would be made to address the concerns of the local population. When asked about a possible Cabinet expansion and other political issues, Omar Abdullah declined to comment, saying his focus during the visit was on development projects and road-related concerns in Beerwah.
